The Missouri River. Flowing approximately two thousand five hundred forty miles from the Rocky Mountains in Montana to its confluence with the Mississippi River near St. Louis, Missouri, the Missouri is technically longer than the Mississippi. Their union creates the enormous downstream flow that characterizes the lower Mississippi valley and drains a vast portion of central North America. The river originates in the Rocky Mountains of western Montana at the confluence of the Gallatin, Jefferson, and Madison Rivers near Three Forks. It was named from the Missouri people, an Amerindian nation who lived along its banks. The term Missouri derives from the native word meaning big muddy or big river, reflecting the river's distinctive characteristics. The Missouri carries enormous sediment loads that give it a murky brown color, and this sediment has historically reshaped the landscape downstream as far as the Mississippi Delta. The river follows a serpentine course eastward across the Great Plains, flowing through or bordering Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Iowa, and Missouri. It served as the primary route of the Lewis and Clark Expedition from eighteen hundred four to eighteen hundred six as they explored western territories and reached the Pacific. The river has been dammed in multiple locations for flood control, hydropower, and irrigation, including the large Fort Peck and Garrison Dams. When it meets the Mississippi just north of St. Louis, the Missouri roughly doubles its volume and determines the character of the lower Mississippi's flow.
